transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, I... I suppose I came because my daughter, Susan, insisted, but she’s right, something is just terribly wrong with me lately. You see, I’ve lived in the same house for forty years, and I’ve always taken such pride in my garden. The roses, the hydrangeas—they’ve always been my joy. But lately... well, just yesterday, the sun was shining so beautifully on the flowerbeds, and Susan brought the grandchildren over. They were sitting right there with me on the patio, laughing and drinking lemonade, just the picture of a perfect afternoon, you know? And I sat there looking at them, and looking at the garden, and I realized... I felt absolutely nothing. It was just... flat. Completely flat inside. It’s like the part of me that used to feel glad, or even just comforted by having my family near me, has just... shut off completely. I don’t know how else to explain it, it’s just a terrible emptiness where the warmth used to be, and it doesn’t matter what they do or how nice the day is, I just can't seem to feel any of the good things anymore.
How long have you been feeling this emptiness and lack of emotional response?

Well, let's see... it hasn't been a lifetime, though it feels like it. It's been about two weeks now. Exactly two weeks this past Tuesday. I remember the day so clearly, doctor, because it was the day everything just... stopped making sense. My husband, Arthur, he was right there in the kitchen with me. We were just having our morning coffee, the way we always do, right at the little table by the window. I had just poured him his second cup, and then... he just collapsed. Right there on the linoleum. And the paramedics, they came so fast, with all their equipment and those heavy boots, and they worked on him right there in our kitchen. They pushed the table out of the way, spilled the coffee everywhere, and I just stood there watching them try to... try to bring him back. And ever since that morning, ever since I watched them working on him on the floor, this... this emptiness just settled into my chest. It hasn't lifted for a single minute in these past two weeks. Not once.
Have you lost interest in activities that you used to enjoy, aside from tending to your garden?

Well, doctor, it's... it's not just the garden, no. It's everything, really. You see, I've always been a part of the Altar Society at St. Jude's, for... oh, it must be nearly fifty years now. Every Thursday morning, a group of us ladies would get together and arrange the flowers for the weekend services, wash the linens, polish the brass—Arthur used to tease me that I spent more time polishing that brass than I did our own silverware. And I loved it, I really did. It was a chance to visit with Mary and Helen, to catch up on the neighborhood news, and to feel like I was doing something useful, something beautiful for the church. 

But this past Thursday... well, I just couldn't bring myself to go. Susan even offered to drive me, said it would be good for me to get out of the house, to see my friends. But the thought of going there, of standing in that quiet church and smelling the lilies... it was just too much, and yet, at the same time, it wasn't enough. I just couldn't see the point of it anymore. And my knitting! I've been knitting a blanket for my newest great-grandson, little Tommy. I had the yarn all picked out, this lovely soft blue, and I was making such good progress. I used to sit in my armchair in the evenings, with the television on low, just knitting away. It was so soothing. But since... since that morning with Arthur, the basket has just been sitting there next to my chair. I look at it, and I know I should pick it up, I know I should want to finish it for the baby, but my hands just feel so heavy. It's like all the things that used to fill up my days, the things that made me who I am, they just don't matter anymore. It's all just... dust. Just dust and empty space.
Have you noticed any significant change in your weight over the past two weeks?

Weight? Oh, well... I haven't really been paying attention to the scale, doctor. I suppose I haven't noticed any big changes, not that I can tell. Though, to be perfectly honest, I haven't been eating the way I used to, either. Arthur always loved a big breakfast, you see. We'd have eggs, and toast with that marmalade he liked—the thick-cut kind from the specialty shop downtown—and bacon. Every single morning, for fifty-something years, I stood at that stove making breakfast. Now... well, Susan comes over and she tries to get me to eat. She brought over a casserole just the other day, chicken and rice, I think it was. She put a portion on a plate and set it right in front of me at the table... but I just stared at it. I took a bite because she was watching me with those worried eyes of hers, but it just tasted like cardboard. I don't feel hungry, you see, but my clothes don't feel any looser, either. I still wear my same slacks and my cardigans, and they fit just the same. So I suppose my weight hasn't changed, even though the thought of sitting down to a proper meal just seems so... impossible right now. It's just too quiet in that kitchen without him, and the food just doesn't seem to matter. I just drink my tea, and sometimes I'll have a cracker if Susan insists, but as for my weight... no, I don't think it's gone up or down, really. It's just everything else that's changed.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to live or harming yourself since your husband passed away?

Oh... oh, no, doctor. No, nothing like that. It's... well, it's a terrible thing to even think about, isn't it? I know some people, when they lose someone they've been with for so long, they just want to follow them right then and there. I remember when my neighbor, Mrs. Gable, lost her husband back in '98—or was it '99? It was right around the time of that terrible ice storm. Anyway, she was just beside herself, saying she couldn't go on, and her daughter had to come stay with her for months. But for me... it's not that I want to harm myself, or that I don't want to live. It's more like... I'm just existing. 

I sit in my chair in the living room—the blue one by the window, not Arthur's recliner, I can't bring myself to sit in his recliner yet—and I just watch the clock tick. The pendulum swings back and forth, back and forth, and I just watch it. I don't want to stop the clock, you understand? I don't want to make it stop ticking. I just... I don't know what to do with the time it's keeping anymore. My faith has always been very important to me, doctor. Father Thomas always says our lives are a gift, and even though Arthur is gone, and even though I feel so incredibly hollow inside, I would never... I would never do anything to end that gift. It's just that the gift feels very heavy right now. I don't want to die, but living just feels like such a long, quiet chore without him here to share it with me. So, no, I haven't had any thoughts of hurting myself. I'm just... waiting, I suppose. Just waiting for the days to pass.
Has your emotional state changed at all over the past two weeks, or has it remained consistently the same since your husband passed away?

Well, no, it hasn't really changed at all, doctor. It’s been exactly like this, just this same... heavy, hollow feeling, for about two weeks now. Ever since that morning. It hasn't lifted for a single minute since my husband collapsed. 

We were just in the kitchen, you see, getting ready for the day just like we always did. I was standing at the sink, rinsing out his coffee mug—the one with the little painted mallard duck on it that Susan got him for Father's Day years and years ago—and I heard this terrible, heavy sound. And then... well, then the paramedics were there. It felt like it took them hours to arrive, though Susan tells me it was only a few minutes. They came rushing in through the side door, tracking dirt all over the linoleum, and they had to shove our breakfast chairs out of the way. The wooden ones with the yellow floral cushions I sewed myself. And they just... they worked on him right there on our kitchen floor. 

I had my back pressed flat against the refrigerator, just watching them press on his chest, listening to them shout all those urgent medical words to each other while the radio was still playing the morning weather report in the background. It was so chaotic, and yet it felt like time was standing completely still. And ever since that exact moment, for these whole two weeks, my mood hasn't shifted one bit. It hasn't gotten any easier, or any different, or any less painful. Every single day I wake up and it's just the exact same gray, quiet feeling... like a part of me is still just stuck right there in the kitchen, leaning against the refrigerator, watching them try to save him. So, no, it hasn't changed. It's just been one long, endless day for two weeks.
Have you felt a depressed mood for most of the day, nearly every day, since your husband passed away?

Well, I wouldn't say "depressed," doctor. Not depressed, exactly. I mean, I know what depression is. My sister, Margaret, she had terrible depression after her youngest moved out to California. She wouldn't get out of bed for weeks, just pulled the curtains tight and let the house go to ruin. Dust everywhere, mail piling up on the porch. I had to go over there twice a week just to make sure she was drinking water. But for me... it's not like that. I still get up. I still get dressed, even if I'm just putting on the same gray cardigan I wore yesterday. 

It's more like... like I said before, it's just this hollowness. I don't sit around crying all day, nearly every day. I don't feel that sort of overwhelming sadness that makes you want to wail and tear your hair out. It's just... flat. Everything is just so incredibly flat. Susan asks me if I'm sad, and I don't even know what to tell her. I'm just... existing in this quiet house. I look out the window at the neighbor's dog running around the yard, and I feel absolutely nothing. I watch the mail carrier drop off the letters, and it doesn't mean a thing to me. 

So, I don't think "depressed" is the right word. I don't feel miserable or despairing most of the day. I just feel... empty. Like a shell of a person just waiting for the sun to go down so I can go back to sleep, only to wake up and do it all over again. But no, I wouldn't call it a depressed mood, not the way you mean it. Just... hollow.
Has your emotional state been like this for less than two months?

Well, yes, less than two months, certainly. Like I mentioned a moment ago, it’s been about two weeks. Exactly two weeks and... well, two weeks and three days, if I'm being precise. Ever since that awful morning. 

It feels like it’s been a lifetime, though, doesn't it? When you're just sitting there, day in and day out, in a house that used to be full of conversation and the smell of Arthur's pipe tobacco—though I always told him he shouldn't smoke it in the house, he'd sneak a puff by the back door anyway. But yes, two weeks. Ever since he collapsed right there on the linoleum. I can still see the paramedics' boots. They were black, heavy boots, the kind with the thick rubber soles, and they left these little scuff marks near the baseboards that I haven't had the heart to scrub away yet. Susan offered to mop the floor for me, bless her heart, but I told her to leave it. It feels strange to erase the last people who were here with him. 

But to answer your question, doctor, yes. It hasn't been two months. It's been just over two weeks of this... this terrible emptiness, ever since they worked on him in the kitchen and couldn't bring him back to me.
Have you experienced any pleasure or enjoyment from activities, hobbies, or social interactions since your husband passed away?

Well, no, doctor. Not at all. That's actually... that's really why I finally agreed to come see you today. Susan was the one who insisted, of course. She said, "Mom, you need to talk to someone, you're just not yourself." And she's right, I suppose, but it's more than just not being myself. It's like... like the part of me that could feel anything good has just completely shut off. 

Just the other day, my grandchildren came over. Little Tommy and Sarah. Usually, seeing them run through the front door, shouting "Grandma!" and dropping their backpacks right in the middle of the hallway—even though I've told them a hundred times to put them in the mudroom—usually, that would just fill my heart right up. Arthur used to scoop them up, both at once, if you can believe it. But this time... they came in, and they were drawing me pictures with those washable markers at the kitchen table, right near where... well, right near the refrigerator. And I sat there with them, and I looked at their little faces, and I just... I felt absolutely nothing. No joy, no comfort. Just that same flat, empty feeling. 

It’s the same with my garden. Arthur and I spent years getting those hydrangeas just right. The soil here is so tricky, you know, you have to add just the right amount of coffee grounds to keep the blooms that beautiful deep blue. And yesterday morning, the sun was shining right on them, hitting the dew on the petals perfectly. It was a picture-perfect morning. But I stood there at the window, holding my tea, and I couldn't feel a single drop of gladness. It’s like I'm completely disconnected from anything that used to bring me happiness. Even when my children sit with me on the sofa, holding my hand, trying to comfort me... the comfort just doesn't reach me. It's just all so flat inside.
Has your condition lasted for most of the day, nearly every day, since your husband passed away?

Well, yes, I suppose it has. Most of the day, nearly every day. It's just... constant. I wake up, usually around 4:30 or 5:00 in the morning—I've always been an early riser, Arthur used to joke that I was part rooster because I couldn't sleep past sunrise—and the emptiness is already there, waiting for me. It sits with me while I make my toast, though I hardly ever finish it anymore. The crusts just sit there on the plate until I throw them out for the birds in the afternoon. 

And it stays with me all through the morning while I watch the clock tick down, waiting for the mail to arrive, not that I care about the mail, but it's something that happens. It's there when Susan calls on her lunch break to check in on me. I try to sound normal for her, I really do, because I know she's worrying herself sick over me. She has enough on her plate with her own children and that new promotion at the bank—she's a branch manager now, you know, very responsible position. But even while I'm talking to her, making all the right noises, I just feel so incredibly hollow. 

And then the afternoon stretches out, and the evening comes, and I sit in Arthur's armchair—I know I shouldn't, I know I should sit in my own chair, but sometimes I just need to be where he was—and the feeling hasn't changed. It hasn't lifted. It doesn't take a break. It's just this heavy, flat nothingness from the moment I open my eyes until I finally manage to drift off to sleep again. So, yes, doctor, it's been like this most of the day, every single day, ever since we lost him. There hasn't been a single hour where I've felt like myself again.
Has your condition lasted for less than three months?

Well, yes, doctor, certainly less than three months. Like I... well, like I think I mentioned when we first sat down together today, it’s been just about two weeks. Two weeks and three days, exactly. I count the days, you see. I actually mark them off on the little floral calendar hanging on the pantry door—the one Arthur always picked up for me from the hardware store downtown at the start of the year. Every morning I wake up and I look at that calendar and I just think, well, there's another day gone by. 

But yes, just two weeks since that awful morning. Since he collapsed right there on the kitchen linoleum. I just can't seem to stop thinking about the paramedics in the kitchen, pulling all their equipment out of those big orange bags... they were rushing around so fast, making so much noise, and one of them knocked over the little wooden step stool I keep by the counter to reach the high cabinets. He didn't even notice, of course, he was just trying so hard to work on Arthur, pressing on his chest and calling out numbers to the other fellow... 

So, yes, to answer your question, nowhere near three months. Just these past two weeks of this terrible feeling, ever since they were working on him right there on our kitchen floor and... well, and that was it.
Have you noticed a lack of interest or pleasure in the things you used to enjoy doing?

Well, yes, doctor... I think that's... well, that's exactly what I was trying to explain when we first started talking today. It's really the main reason I finally agreed to come in and sit in this chair. Like I mentioned earlier about my garden, and about the grandchildren coming over... those things used to be my entire world. I used to spend hours out in the dirt, you know, and I'd bake these little almond cookies Arthur loved whenever the kids came by. 

But now... well, it's exactly like I was saying before. Even when my own children are sitting right there next to me on the sofa, holding my hand, trying so incredibly hard to comfort me... or when the sun is shining so beautifully right on my garden... I just feel completely flat inside. Nothing at all. It truly feels like... like the part of me that could ever be glad about anything, or the part that could be comforted by my family, has just completely shut off. I don't even have the desire to look out the window at the yard anymore, let alone go out and prune the bushes. The interest in all of it is just entirely gone, doctor. Just swept away.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since your husband passed away?

Weight? Oh, well, I don't... I don't really know, doctor. I haven't stepped on the scale, honestly. The scale is in the upstairs bathroom, the one with the blue tiles that Arthur put in back in '85, and I just... I haven't been up there much. I sleep in the guest room downstairs now, because walking past our bedroom door is just too hard. 

But as for my weight... I suppose I might have lost a little, but I couldn't say if it's a significant amount. Like I mentioned earlier, I hardly finish my toast in the mornings anymore. And Susan keeps bringing over these casseroles—bless her heart, she brought a tuna noodle one just yesterday, the kind with the crushed potato chips on top that the kids always liked—but I just take a few bites and push it around the plate. I just don't have the appetite. The food tastes like cardboard, really. But I haven't noticed my clothes falling off me or anything drastic like that. I wear these loose house dresses most days anyway, the comfortable cotton ones I usually order from that catalog that comes in the spring... so it's hard to tell if they're fitting any differently. I just... I really haven't paid any attention to my weight, doctor. There are just so many other things crowding my mind right now.
Do you feel like you have no interest in doing things that you used to enjoy?

Well, yes, doctor... I believe you asked me something very similar just a few moments ago, didn't you? About my interests and the things I used to enjoy? Yes, I'm quite sure we just spoke about this. It's exactly like I was saying before... all the joy is just gone. 

I was telling you about the garden, remember? And my grandchildren. Those were the things that filled my days. I used to wake up and practically rush through my morning tea just so I could get out there and check on my hydrangeas. Arthur always said I loved those hydrangeas more than him, which wasn't true, of course, but it was a little joke between us. He'd sit on the patio with his crossword puzzle while I was on my knees in the dirt with my gardening gloves... the green ones with the little yellow daisies printed on them. 

But now, just like I explained to you a minute ago, I can't even bring myself to look out that back window. The thought of going out there, or even baking those cookies for the kids... it's just completely empty for me now. The feeling is just completely gone. I just sit in the house and watch the clock, honestly. I don't want to do any of it anymore. I thought I made that clear when we were talking about it just before... it's like a light switch was flipped off inside me, doctor. Just completely off.
Do you feel like there's anything you still enjoy or look forward to?

Doctor, I... well, I feel like I keep saying the very same thing over and over, don't I? Are you writing all this down in your notes? Because I honestly don't know how else to explain it to you. 

Like I was just saying, the whole reason I finally let my daughter Susan drive me here today—she had to take the entire morning off from her job at the bank, you know, which she really shouldn't do with the holidays coming up—but the main reason I came in is because of this exact thing. There is absolutely nothing I look forward to. Nothing at all. I was telling you about my children sitting with me, trying to hold my hand on the sofa... the floral sofa in the living room that Arthur and I picked out together... and even when they are right there, doing their very best to comfort their mother, or when the sun is shining right on my beautiful garden out back, I just feel so terribly flat inside. 

It's a dreadful feeling, doctor, just... complete nothingness. I look at my kids, and I look at the sun on the yard, and I know in my head that I should feel something, some little spark of gladness or at least some comfort that I'm not alone, but I just don't. It's exactly like I said before, that part of me... the part that could ever be glad about a visit from the family or comforted by a warm hug... it has just completely shut off. The switch is off, and the wires are cut. So no, doctor, to answer your question again, there is absolutely nothing I enjoy or look forward to anymore. I really don't know how to make it any clearer than I already have.
Has your condition lasted for more than two weeks but less than two months?

Well, let's see... two weeks, you said? Yes, I suppose it's been right about exactly two weeks now. It feels like a lifetime, honestly, but if I look at the calendar, it's been just about two weeks. 

It all started... well, it started the day Arthur collapsed. It was a Tuesday, I remember because the garbage trucks had just come by and I was thinking about how I needed to bring the bins back up the driveway before it rained. I was standing right there by the sink, washing the breakfast dishes—the blue willow pattern ones we've had forever—and he just... he just went down. Right there on the linoleum. 

And then the paramedics came, two young men, they looked so young, like they should still be in high school, and they were working on him right there on the kitchen floor. Between the island and the refrigerator. They had all their equipment spread out, and the radio was crackling, and I just stood there in the doorway holding a wet dishcloth. I couldn't move. I couldn't even breathe, it felt like. 

So yes, it's been going on since that morning. Two weeks of this... this terrible emptiness. It hasn't been a month or two months, no, just these past fourteen days since I watched them try to save him right there on my kitchen floor. Every single day since then has just been exactly like I've been telling you.
Has your condition lasted for less than six months?

Doctor, I... well, I feel like we are just going in circles now, aren't we? I really do. Because, as I just finished explaining to you not two minutes ago, it has been exactly two weeks. Two weeks since that awful Tuesday morning. 

So when you ask me if it's been less than six months... well, yes, of course it has. It hasn't been six months, it hasn't been six weeks, it hasn't been anything close to that. It's been fourteen days. Fourteen very long, very empty days since I stood there with that wet dishcloth in my hand watching those young paramedics on my kitchen floor. I really thought I made that quite clear just a moment ago. 

I know you have your questions to get through, and Susan told me I needed to be patient and just answer whatever you asked, but I honestly don't understand why you keep asking me about the timeframe when I've just told you exactly when it started. It was the Tuesday the garbage trucks came, two weeks ago today. I remember the sound of the truck backing up the street just before he fell. The backup beep, beep, beep... it was so loud, and then just... silence in the house. So yes, doctor, less than six months. Much less. Just two weeks. Are we going to keep talking about the calendar, or is there something else you need to know?
Do you feel sad most of the day?

Sad? No, I... well, I wouldn't use that word, doctor. I know that's what everyone expects, of course. Susan keeps bringing me boxes of Kleenex, leaving them in every single room of the house—there's a box on the coffee table, one by the telephone in the hallway, one on my nightstand right next to Arthur's reading lamp... she just expects me to be weeping all day long. But I'm not. 

If I were sad, wouldn't I be crying? When my neighbor Martha lost her husband George—oh, this must have been back in 1998 or so, maybe '99—she just sobbed for months. She was terribly, terribly sad. You could hear her through the fence when I was out watering the hydrangeas. But for me, it's... it's not sadness at all. It's just that complete nothingness I was trying to explain to you earlier. 

I sit there in the living room, sometimes I'll even sit right in Arthur's chair, the burgundy leather recliner we got from Sears for his retirement, and I just stare at the grandfather clock. I don't feel like crying. I don't feel a heavy heart, or whatever they call it in the movies or the greeting cards. I have these beautiful embroidered handkerchiefs my mother left me, sitting right in the top drawer of my dresser, but I haven't shed a single tear to need them. I just feel completely hollowed out, like someone took a scoop and just emptied out my chest. 

So if you're asking if I sit around feeling sad and weeping most of the day, no, I don't. I don't feel much of anything at all, just that terrible flat feeling. I really thought we had already covered how empty it all is. Do you see what I mean? It's not sadness, doctor, it's just... nothing.
Has your condition lasted for more than one month?

Doctor, I... I really must ask, are you listening to me? Are you writing any of this down in your little notepad there? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall sometimes. We just went over this. We talked about the two weeks, we talked about the six months, and now you're asking me about a month? 

No, it has not been more than a month. It has been two weeks. Exactly two weeks. I don't know how many different ways I can say it. It was the Tuesday the garbage trucks came, two weeks ago today. I was standing by the sink, washing the blue willow dishes, and Arthur collapsed on the linoleum. And then the young paramedics came and worked on him right there in the kitchen, between the island and the refrigerator. 

That was two weeks ago. Fourteen days. Not a month. Not more than a month. Just two weeks of this awful, hollow feeling. I honestly don't understand why we keep coming back to the calendar, doctor. I've told you when it happened. I've told you what happened. Are we going to keep asking about the timeline, or are we going to talk about something else? Because I'm getting quite tired of repeating myself. Susan told me to be patient, she really did, she said, "Now Mother, you just answer the nice doctor's questions," but I feel like I'm losing my mind having to say "two weeks" over and over again. It has been two weeks. Not a month. Two weeks.
Has your lack of interest in activities and feelings of emptiness been present for most of every day?

Yes... yes, it's most of every day. It's all day, really. From the moment I open my eyes in the morning until I finally manage to drift off at night. That's actually why Susan finally insisted I come see you, doctor. Because it just never lifts. Not for a minute. 

Susan came over on Sunday—she usually comes on Sundays, brings a roast or sometimes a nice chicken, she knows Arthur loved a roasted chicken with those little red potatoes—and she brought the grandchildren. Little Timmy and Sarah. Usually, when those children walk through the front door, my heart just lights up. Timmy is seven now, and he always runs straight to the kitchen to see if I've made those oatmeal cookies he likes, the ones with the raisins that I soak in warm water first so they get nice and plump. And Sarah, she's five, she always wants to show me her drawings. 

But this past Sunday... they came in, and they were running around, and Susan had brought this beautiful bouquet of yellow tulips, my absolute favorites, and she put them right there on the dining room table where the sun hits them in the afternoon. And I sat there, looking at my grandchildren, looking at the sun shining on my garden out the bay window, looking at those bright yellow flowers... and nothing. Absolutely nothing. 

I came because even when my children sit with me, even when the sun is on my garden and the house is full of the people I love most in this world, I just feel completely flat inside. It's like... it's like the part of me that could be glad, or comforted, or even just warmed by a hug from my grandson... it just shut off. Like someone flipped a switch in the breaker box down in the basement and all the power to that part of my heart just went out. So yes, doctor, it's every day, most of the day. It never stops being empty. I just can't feel any joy at all, no matter what is happening around me.

You could hear her through the fence when I was out watering the hydrangeas. But for me, it's... it's not sadness at all. It's just that complete nothingness I was trying to explain to you earlier. 

I sit there in the living room, sometimes I'll even sit right in Arthur's chair, the burgundy leather recliner we got from Sears for his retirement, and I just stare at the grandfather clock. I don't feel like crying. I don't feel a heavy heart, or whatever they call it in the movies or the greeting cards. I have these beautiful embroidered handkerchiefs my mother left me, sitting right in the top drawer of my dresser, but I haven't shed a single tear to need them. I just feel completely hollowed out, like someone took a scoop and just emptied out my chest. 

So if you're asking if I sit around feeling sad and weeping most of the day, no, I don't. I don't feel much of anything at all, just that terrible flat feeling. I really thought we had already covered how empty it all is. Do you see what I mean? It's not sadness, doctor, it's just... nothing.

doctor.question: Has your condition lasted for more than one month?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about two weeks, ever since my husband collapsed and the paramedics worked on him in our kitchen.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the condition has lasted for more than one month, which is directly inquiring about the duration of the symptoms.

patient.answer:
Doctor, I... I really must ask, are you listening to me? Are you writing any of this down in your little notepad there? Because I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall sometimes. We just went over this. We talked about the two weeks, we talked about the six months, and now you're asking me about a month? 

No, it has not been more than a month. It has been two weeks. Exactly two weeks. I don't know how many different ways I can say it. It was the Tuesday the garbage trucks came, two weeks ago today. I was standing by the sink, washing the blue willow dishes, and Arthur collapsed on the linoleum. And then the young paramedics came and worked on him right there in the kitchen, between the island and the refrigerator. 

That was two weeks ago. Fourteen days. Not a month. Not more than a month. Just two weeks of this awful, hollow feeling. I honestly don't understand why we keep coming back to the calendar, doctor. I've told you when it happened. I've told you what happened. Are we going to keep asking about the timeline, or are we going to talk about something else? Because I'm getting quite tired of repeating myself. Susan told me to be patient, she really did, she said, "Now Mother, you just answer the nice doctor's questions," but I feel like I'm losing my mind having to say "two weeks" over and over again. It has been two weeks. Not a month. Two weeks.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition meets the duration criteria for a specific diagnosis
doctor.question: Has your lack of interest in activities and feelings of emptiness been present for most of every day?

target_item.name: Inability_Positive_Emotions
target_item.manifestation: I came because even when my children sit with me or the sun is on my garden, I feel flat inside, like the part of me that could be glad or comforted just shut off.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the frequency and persistence of my feelings of emptiness and lack of interest, which directly relates to my inability to experience positive emotions.

patient.answer:
Yes... yes, it's most of every day. It's all day, really. From the moment I open my eyes in the morning until I finally manage to drift off at night. That's actually why Susan finally insisted I come see you, doctor. Because it just never lifts. Not for a minute. 

Susan came over on Sunday—she usually comes on Sundays, brings a roast or sometimes a nice chicken, she knows Arthur loved a roasted chicken with those little red potatoes—and she brought the grandchildren. Little Timmy and Sarah. Usually, when those children walk through the front door, my heart just lights up. Timmy is seven now, and he always runs straight to the kitchen to see if I've made those oatmeal cookies he likes, the ones with the raisins that I soak in warm water first so they get nice and plump. And Sarah, she's five, she always wants to show me her drawings. 

But this past Sunday... they came in, and they were running around, and Susan had brought this beautiful bouquet of yellow tulips, my absolute favorites, and she put them right there on the dining room table where the sun hits them in the afternoon. And I sat there, looking at my grandchildren, looking at the sun shining on my garden out the bay window, looking at those bright yellow flowers... and nothing. Absolutely nothing. 

I came because even when my children sit with me, even when the sun is on my garden and the house is full of the people I love most in this world, I just feel completely flat inside. It's like... it's like the part of me that could be glad, or comforted, or even just warmed by a hug from my grandson... it just shut off. Like someone flipped a switch in the breaker box down in the basement and all the power to that part of my heart just went out. So yes, doctor, it's every day, most of the day. It never stops being empty. I just can't feel any joy at all, no matter what is happening around me.
